gender.3.why: Divides abolitionist/Nordic-model camps (punish only the buyer) from libertarians who see a voluntary contract and from moral-order and sharia camps that would punish both parties; feminists split between Nordic-model and decriminalisation.

notes.RF: Radical feminism built the Nordic model: buying sex is male violence, the seller is a victim (Dworkin, MacKinnon).
notes.NM: Sweden 1999 Sex Purchase Act, copied by Norway and Iceland, is the origin of buyer-only punishment.
notes.LF: Voluntary exchange between adults is not a crime on either side (Rothbard, Mises-style contract freedom).
notes.PE: Ngo Dinh Nhu and Madame Nhu banned brothels and criminalised the trade as a whole (1962 Family Law), so both sides are punished.
notes.VEF: Zina is a hadd offence for both parties under Iranian law, so buyer-only is rejected.
notes.LIF: Liberal feminists are split: Amnesty-style decriminalisation vs Nordic model; most typical lean is against singling out one party.

identity.culture.5.why: Cultural continuity as the test of a nation's survival: cultural, ethnic and religious nationalists agree strongly, while cosmopolitan, individualist and internationalist-Marxist camps see culture as no measure of a people's existence.

notes.CN: Herder and the cultural nationalists locate the nation in language and customs rather than the state, so a people with its culture is not lost (cf. Phan Chu Trinh-era Vietnamese slogan about language and nation).
notes.SN: Stateless nations (Catalans, Kurds, Scots) hold that survival of language and culture keeps the nation alive without a state.
notes.RS: Vietnamese Party line since Resolution 5 (1998): an advanced culture imbued with national identity (tien tien, dam da ban sac dan toc).
notes.CF: Cosmopolitan federalists treat cultural distinctiveness as no test of nationhood and prioritise individual and world citizenship.
notes.JA: Jacobins suppressed regional languages (Gregoire report 1794) to forge one national culture, so cultural difference does not make a people.
notes.LU: Luxemburg rejected national self-determination as bourgeois ideology; class not culture defines peoples.

nature-of-man.5.why: Moral decline versus moral progress: traditionalists, religious revivalists, communitarians and golden-age Confucians/Taoists say yes; progressives, liberals, Marxists, ecomodernists and transhumanists see moral progress.

notes.RT: Traditionalism of Guenon and Evola holds the Kali Yuga: history is a descent from a primordial Golden Age, so decline is doctrine.
notes.TW: Laozi: when the Dao is lost virtue appears, then benevolence, then ritual; civilisation is a decline from natural simplicity.
notes.LE: Han Fei mocks reverence for the ancients: different ages need different rules, and the old kings were not morally better.
notes.RS: Vietnamese Party documents repeatedly speak of suy thoai dao duc, loi song (degeneration of morality and lifestyle) in society today.
notes.EM: Ecomodernist Manifesto and Pinker-style moral progress: violence and cruelty have fallen over history.
notes.CLR: Machiavelli/Polybius: republics decay through loss of civic virtue, a cyclical decline of corruption.

notes.LEG: Legitimism holds the hereditary dynastic right of the crown as the core of political legitimacy (Bourbon, Stuart lines).
notes.KS: Arthashastra is a manual for the rajan; monarchy is the only form it conceives.
notes.VEF: Khomeini in Islamic Government: Islam and monarchy are contradictory, so guardianship of the jurist replaces the shah.
notes.SR: French Radicals were republican by doctrine; the Republic itself was their programme against crown and Church.
notes.PAL: Hoppe (Democracy: The God That Failed) argues hereditary monarchy beats democracy for private-property order.
notes.KE: Ataturk abolished the sultanate (1922) and proclaimed the republic (1923), a founding act of Kemalism.
notes.RS: Vietnamese socialist republic: the Party line is anti-monarchy since 1945 abdication of Bao Dai.

distribution.labour.8.why: Individual wage bargaining with no third party: market liberals and libertarians agree, while Marxists, corporatists, Catholic social teaching, social democracy and populists want unions, collective bargaining, state minimums or wage planning.

notes.LF: Laissez-faire holds wage contracts are voluntary exchange; minimum wages and union privileges are interference.
notes.CST: Rerum Novarum (1891) says a wage is not just merely because freely agreed; a living family wage is owed whatever the contract.
notes.POC: The Dutch polder (Wassenaar Accord 1982) is built on tripartite wage coordination between unions, employers and state.
notes.NAZ: Nazi Labour Trustees (Treuhaender der Arbeit) set wages by decree after unions were abolished.
notes.AL: Authoritarian liberalism (Schmitt, Hayek-style) wants a strong state that keeps wage-setting a market matter by suppressing union pressure.
notes.NM: Nordic wage-setting is collective bargaining between union and employer federations, not individual deals; adherents would reject the item as worded.

notes.RS: Vietnamese Constitution (Art. 53) says land belongs to the entire people with the State as representative owner, so the item is near-verbatim doctrine.

nature-of-man.1.why: Innate goodness versus fallenness: Mencius, Buddhist-nature, Rousseauian and anarchist-communist views say yes; Xunzi, Han Fei, Hobbes, Calvinists, Burkeans and reactionaries say no; Marxists and many economic schools treat nature as socially formed and sit near neutral.

notes.MC: Mencius 6A: human nature is good as water flows downward, the doctrinal foundation of benevolent government.
notes.XC: Xunzi: human nature is bad (xing e); goodness is artifice made by ritual and teachers.
notes.HS: Hobbes Leviathan ch. 13: the natural condition is war of all against all, driven by competition, diffidence and glory.
notes.CT: Total depravity in Reformed doctrine: humans are born sinful and cannot choose good without grace.
notes.JA: Rousseau, Jacobin teacher: man is born good and corrupted by society.
notes.AC: Kropotkin Mutual Aid: cooperation is a natural factor of evolution, so people are social by nature.
notes.EB: Engaged Buddhism builds on Buddha-nature, the inherent awakened potential in every being (Thich Nhat Hanh).

class.5.why: Whether religious community outranks class solidarity: Islamist, integralist and religious-Zionist camps say faith binds more, while every Marxist and anarchist camp holds class (or the nation, for Kemalists and Baathists) comes first.

notes.VEF: The ummah is the primary bond in Islamic political thought; Khomeini opposed class-struggle framing in favour of Islamic unity.
notes.IB: Qutb and the Brotherhood: belonging is by creed (aqida), not class or ethnicity.
notes.ML: Marxism-Leninism: religion is a distraction from class interest; workers of all faiths unite and religious solidarity with exploiters is false consciousness.
notes.KE: Kemalism replaced the religious ummah identity with secular Turkish nationhood, rejecting both faith and class as primary bonds.
notes.CI: Integralism sees the Catholic body as the true political community, cutting across rank and class.
notes.LT: Liberation theology links faith to solidarity with the poor, so faith and class fuse; adherents split on which comes first.

change.pace.4.why: Decisive, irreversible reform versus gradualism: revolutionaries, shock-therapy liberals and Legalists say strike once and for all; Burkeans, Fabians, consensus and social-market schools prefer step-by-step change, and restorationists reject irreversibility itself.

notes.LE: Book of Lord Shang: a ruler who hesitates in reform cannot succeed; Shang Yang overturned the old order in one sweep.
notes.FA: Fabian doctrine of the inevitability of gradualness (Webb): permeation and step-by-step reform, not a single rupture.
notes.BC: Burke Reflections: reform must be gradual and preserve what exists; sweeping change destroys the inheritance.
notes.KE: Kemalist reforms (abolition of the caliphate, alphabet and dress laws) were imposed rapidly to foreclose return.
notes.RS: Doi Moi and Deng-style reform proceeded by experiment (crossing the river by feeling the stones), so adherents lean gradual.
notes.JA: Jacobins pursued irreversible rupture (Terror, revolutionary calendar) so that the old regime could never return.
notes.LEG: Legitimism aims precisely at restoring the old order, so irreversibility of reform is what it opposes.

nature-of-man.3.why: Material progress: liberals, social democrats, Marxists, ecomodernists and transhumanists say life is better today; primitivists, traditionalists, reactionaries and golden-age moralists say it is worse.

notes.EM: Ecomodernist Manifesto celebrates falling poverty, mortality and violence as human progress.
notes.GA: Zerzan and Jensen: civilisation brings alienation and domination; pre-agricultural life was better, so the item is rejected as doctrine.
notes.COR: Throne-and-altar reaction (de Maistre, Bonald) reads the post-1789 world as a fall from Christian order.
notes.GAN: Hind Swaraj calls modern civilisation a disease; Gandhi preferred village simplicity to industrial progress.
notes.TRA: Transhumanism rests on improvement of the human condition through technology as an ongoing historical trend.
notes.LE: Han Fei: the present age is better suited and the ancients were no model, a progress-minded Legalism.

religion.law.5.why: One civil marriage law for all faiths: secularists, Marxists, Kemalists, Hindu nationalists (Uniform Civil Code) and French-style republicans agree, while sharia states, Calvinist reconstruction, Catholic integralists and religious Zionists want marriage governed by religious law.

notes.HI: A Uniform Civil Code for all Indians is a long-standing core demand of Hindutva (RSS/BJP), aimed at Muslim personal law.
notes.KE: The 1926 Swiss-derived Civil Code replaced sharia family law with one secular marriage law for all Turks.
notes.VEF: Marriage and family are governed by the jurist-interpreted sharia; Iranian personal-status courts apply religion-specific law.
notes.CI: Integralism subordinates civil marriage law to canon law for the baptised; a religion-blind marriage code is rejected.
notes.SR: French Radicals made civil marriage and laicite their signature cause; the republic knows citizens, not confessions.
notes.RZ: Religious Zionism upholds Orthodox rabbinate control of Jewish marriage in Israel, so a faith-blind code is opposed.
notes.MA: The 1950 PRC Marriage Law abolished arranged and religious-customary marriage in favour of one law for all citizens.

foreign.intervention.7.why: Unconditional aid: non-aligned, anti-imperialist and sovereigntist camps (Bandung, Eight Principles of Chinese aid, Chavista ALBA, Juche) reject political strings, while liberal-interventionist, neoconservative and Nordic or social-liberal schools want aid tied to governance and rights.

notes.NOA: Bandung Principles (1955) require non-interference in internal affairs, which condemns conditionality as neocolonial.
notes.MA: Zhou Enlai Eight Principles of Foreign Aid (1964): aid carries no conditions and no privileges.
notes.LI: Liberal interventionism ties aid and force to democracy and rights; conditionality is its instrument.
notes.CH: ALBA and Petrocaribe offered oil and aid explicitly outside IMF-style conditionality.
notes.KS: Kautilya mandala theory treats gifts and aid as tools of leverage over neighbours, so unconditional giving is rejected.
notes.LIF: Liberal feminists back tying aid to women rights and governance reforms (gender conditionality in Western donor policy).
